title: Logic and Reasoning
description: Work out what follows from what. Read arguments carefully, test them against cases, and see where everyday reasoning goes wrong.
audience: A general reader with no background in formal logic who wants to argue and evaluate arguments more carefully.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Logical Consequence

modules.title: Deduction
modules.summary: What it means for a conclusion to follow from its premises, and how to test whether it does.

concepts.title: Statement
concepts.summary: A sentence that is either true or false, which is what logic operates on.

concepts.title: Conditional
concepts.summary: An if-then claim, which is false only when the antecedent holds and the consequent fails.

concepts.title: Truth table
concepts.summary: An exhaustive listing of the cases a compound statement can take.

concepts.title: Negation and converse
concepts.summary: Turning a conditional around or inside out changes what it claims.

lessons.title: What logic operates on
lessons.outcome: Tell statements apart from questions, commands and opinions, and say why only statements can be premises.
outline: Hook: offer four sentences and ask which could be true or false
Explain what makes a sentence a statement
Definition: statement, truth value
Worked example: sorting borderline sentences
Check: classify a sentence that looks like a claim but is not
Close: only statements can carry an argument

lessons.title: If-then claims
lessons.outcome: State exactly when a conditional is false, and resist the pull to read it as a promise about the antecedent.
outline: Hook: predict when 'if it rains, the match is cancelled' is broken
Explain the four cases
Equation-free truth table for the conditional
Worked example: a true conditional with a false antecedent
Check: pick the only case that falsifies it
Close: a conditional says nothing when its antecedent fails

lessons.title: Converse and contrapositive
lessons.outcome: Recognise that a conditional and its contrapositive say the same thing, while its converse does not.
outline: Hook: does 'all cats are mammals' mean 'all mammals are cats'?
Explain converse, inverse and contrapositive
Worked example: the contrapositive of a familiar rule
Interact: match each transformation to its meaning
Check: spot the illegitimate flip
Close: only the contrapositive is guaranteed

lessons.title: Knights and knaves
lessons.outcome: Solve a small puzzle by assuming a case and following it to a contradiction.
outline: Hook: one islander says 'we are both knaves'
Explain proof by cases
Worked example: assume the speaker is a knight and see what breaks
Interact: tap the islander whose statement settles it
Check: a two-speaker puzzle
Close: contradiction is a tool, not a failure

lessons.title: Building a truth table
lessons.outcome: Enumerate the cases of a two-variable compound statement and read validity off the result.
outline: Hook: how many rows does a two-variable table need?
Explain enumeration and why the count doubles
Worked example: and, or, not side by side
Interact: order the rows of a table correctly
Check: identify which row breaks an argument
Close: exhaustion beats intuition on small problems

modules.title: Arguments
modules.summary: Telling a good argument from a persuasive one, and naming the ways reasoning fails.

concepts.title: Premise and conclusion
concepts.summary: The claims offered as support, and the claim they are meant to support.

concepts.title: Validity and soundness
concepts.summary: Whether the conclusion follows, and separately whether the premises are true.

concepts.title: Fallacy
concepts.summary: A pattern of reasoning that persuades without supporting.

lessons.title: Finding the conclusion
lessons.outcome: Separate an argument's conclusion from the claims offered in its support.
outline: Hook: a short paragraph with the conclusion buried in the middle
Explain indicator words and the 'therefore' test
Worked example: reordering a paragraph into premises and conclusion
Interact: order the claims from support to conclusion
Check: pick the conclusion of an unfamiliar passage
Close: find the conclusion before judging the argument

lessons.title: Valid but untrue
lessons.outcome: Judge whether a conclusion follows separately from whether the premises are true.
outline: Hook: an argument with absurd premises and a watertight structure
Explain validity as a property of form
Definition: soundness
Worked example: four arguments across the valid/true grid
Check: classify an argument that is valid and unsound
Close: two questions, asked separately

lessons.title: Naming the fallacies
lessons.outcome: Identify affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent, and attacking the person.
outline: Hook: an argument that feels right and is not
Explain affirming the consequent against the conditional's truth table
Explain denying the antecedent
Worked example: the same fallacy in a news sentence
Interact: match arguments to the fallacy they commit
Check: the one argument that is actually valid
Close: a named mistake is easier to notice
